MC Strategy

70 questions, 120 minutes: just under 2 minutes each — but the real math is easier: the exam is 57 short single-selects, 5 passage questions, and 8 multi-selects. Most short questions take 45-90 seconds. Bank that time for the passages and the grid questions.

Pacing plan

  1. Pass 1 (about 80 min): every question in order. Answer every one you are confident in; star and skip anything that makes you stall.
  2. Pass 2 (about 30 min): the starred ones, hardest first — you are warmed up now.
  3. Pass 3 (about 10 min): bubbles checked, guesses made. Never leave a question blank — there is no penalty for guessing.

The question types

  • Single-select (57): four choices, one right. Mostly code reading: "what does this pseudocode display?" — trace it like we traced the enemy state machine.
  • Passage (5): a paragraph about a computing innovation, then questions about benefits, harms, data, and bias. Read the questions FIRST, then skim the passage for the answers.
  • Multi-select (8): pick exactly TWO of four. You need both for full credit. If you only see one that is right, the other is usually the "obvious but wrong" twin — find the one the question is really about.

The trap catalog (learn the traps, dodge them for free)

TrapLooks likeDodge
Off-by-oneREPEAT 5 TIMES vs a list of length 5; index 5 is out of rangeCount on your fingers. Literally.
Integer vs decimal division3/2 displays 1, not 1.5, in the exam's pseudocodeKnow the reference sheet's rules — they differ from C#!
Reversed logic"Displays the number of values GREATER than x" — the answer choice counts less-thanUnderline the comparison word in the stem.
Not-quite-loopsA loop that runs but never updates the counter → infiniteCheck the update line before anything else.
Bandwidth vs latency"Faster download" answers on a question about pingBandwidth = how much per second; latency = how long until the first byte.
Lossless vs lossy"ZIP restores exactly" vs "JPEG restores close enough"ZIP/PNG/GIF = lossless; JPEG/MP3/streaming video = lossy.
Correlation vs causation"Games cause grades" from a datasetPattern ≠ cause. That is the whole answer choice.
Phishing vs virus vs DDoSMixed-up threat typesPhishing = social engineering; DDoS = traffic flood; malware = code.

Using our clinics

May 5-13 we run three full practice sets + one written-response drill. Score your own work, tag every miss with its trap from the catalog above, and bring the top three to the next clinic. The last week is for fixing YOUR specific leaks, not for more content.
